html:
Francisco Vázquez de Coronado was a Spanish conquistador who led a great expedition from Mexico into what is now the southwestern United States and the Great Plains, from 1540 to 1542.

Born in Salamanca, he went to New Spain in 1535 and became governor of a province in the northwest. Reports from the friar Marcos de Niza and the African explorer Estevanico spoke of seven rich cities, Cíbola, to the north. In 1540 Coronado set out with a few hundred Spaniards and well over a thousand Indigenous allies from Mexico, passing through the lands of the Ópata.

  • In July 1540 he took Hawikuh, a town of the Zuni, by force. There was no gold.
  • Side parties reached the Hopi towns and the Grand Canyon.
  • He wintered among the Tiwa towns on the Rio Grande, among the Pueblo peoples, where his demands for food and clothing led to war and the burning of captives.
  • In 1541 a guide led him across the plains to Quivira in Kansas, which proved to be grass-house villages of the Wichita.

He came back empty-handed in 1542, was tried for cruelty to the Native peoples and cleared, and died in Mexico City in 1554. His journey gave the Spanish their first picture of the interior of North America.
